reasoning_notes: For each candidate I matched its events to the best-fitting causal chain and checked three things in order of weight: (1) CAUSAL ORDER - do the first_seen_day values of the present events increase in the same sequence the chain dictates? Any inversion (e.g. component_defect before supplier_substitution, contract_penalty before sla_breach, forecast_revision before margin_compression) was treated as a strong artefact signal even when source/site counts were high, since a real cascade can't run backwards. This caught several high-volume 'trap' candidates (C-20, C-24) that looked impressive on raw counts but were badly scrambled. (2) PER-LINK CORROBORATION - within an order-consistent chain, I required every individual link to have independent_sources >= 2 (i.e. no stage resting on a single report from a single site); chains with even one single-source link were downgraded, and a candidate where literally every link had exactly 1 source/1 site (C-35) was flagged as the clearest 'single report' artefact. (3) LOUD-SITE PATTERN - a large gap between total_reports and independent_sources combined with a small, unchanging distinct_sites count across links (C-26: 17/15/16 reports from only 5-6 sources, 3 sites each) signals one site's repetitive routine traffic rather than organisation-wide spread, so it was ranked near the bottom despite correct ordering. Secondary tie-breakers: chain completeness (more of the 4-6 stage chain represented), total distinct_sites/regions covered, and contradiction_count. I also noticed four entity names appear twice (arbor-hub, nimbusx532, meridian-eu, basalt-net) with one instance forming a clean ordered chain and the other a weaker/inverted one on a different chain - treated as a real/decoy pair and scored independently on the same criteria, which correctly separated them (e.g. C-12 nimbusx532 ranked #1 while its C-37 namesake with an order inversion fell into the bottom artefact tier).
